questions.question: What does the Arabic word 'dabh' in the opening verse of Surah Al-Adiyat describe?
options: The thunder of distant clouds
The heavy panting and snorting of horses at full gallop
The clatter of swords in battle
The footsteps of pilgrims rushing to Arafat
questions.explanation: Layer 1 explains that 'dabh' is the heavy breathing and snorting of a horse pushed to its full speed, a sound the Arabs of the Prophet's time recognized immediately and which is uniquely associated with horses charging in battle.

questions.question: True or false: Imam Tabari and the majority of classical Sunni scholars held that 'al-adiyat' refers to war-horses charging in jihad rather than camels of pilgrims.
questions.explanation: Tabari, Ibn Kathir, and the majority of classical scholars of the Salaf adhered to the war-horse interpretation, citing Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid, and Ikrimah, and noting that 'dabh' is a sound uniquely associated with horses, not camels.

questions.question: Why did Tabari and Ibn Kathir argue that the war-horse interpretation fits verse two ('al-muriyat qadha') better than the camel interpretation?
options: Because camels move faster than horses on rocky ground
Because camels were more common in Mecca than horses
Because camel hooves do not typically produce sparks the way iron-shod horse hooves do
Because the verse mentions weapons that only cavalry carried
questions.explanation: Layer 2 records that classical scholars who took 'al-adiyat' as camels struggled to explain this verse, since camel hooves do not produce sparks as iron-shod horse hooves do — a point Tabari and Ibn Kathir used to support the war-horse reading as linguistically and contextually superior.

questions.question: True or false: The word 'subha' in verse three indicates that the cavalry charge takes place at midday when visibility is greatest.
questions.explanation: Layer 1 explains that 'subha' means at dawn or in the early morning. The dawn raid was the most feared and effective military strategy in ancient Arabian warfare because of the element of surprise and the disorienting half-light of early morning.

questions.question: How did al-Hasan al-Basri famously define the word 'kanud' in verse six?
options: One who never prays at night
One who counts his calamities and forgets his blessings
One who refuses to fight in battle
One who hides his wealth from the poor
questions.explanation: Al-Hasan al-Basri's definition of 'kanud' as 'the one who counts his calamities and forgets his blessings' is preserved in both Tabari's Jami al-Bayan and Ibn Kathir's tafsir as a particularly insightful elaboration on the nature of human ingratitude.

questions.question: True or false: Sayyid Qutb argued that modern consumer culture institutionalises the very disease of intense love of wealth (hubb al-khayr) that the Quran diagnoses in verse eight.
questions.explanation: In Fi Zilal al-Quran, Sayyid Qutb argued that modern industrialised societies have elevated the acquisition of wealth and material comfort to a supreme life-goal, effectively institutionalising the love of khayr that verse eight identifies as the root of ingratitude.

questions.question: According to the majority Sunni reading recorded by Tabari and Ibn Kathir, who is the 'witness' (shahid) referred to in verse seven?
options: The angels who record human deeds
The Prophet Muhammad on the Day of Judgment
The human being himself, who knows his own ingratitude
The earth, which will testify on Judgment Day
questions.explanation: Tabari and Ibn Kathir lean toward the reading that mankind is the witness against himself — he knows his own ingratitude and cannot claim ignorance. Ibn Kathir reinforces this with the parallel verse Al-Qiyamah 75:14: 'Rather, man will be a witness against himself.'

questions.question: What does the Arabic verb 'bu'thira' in verse nine convey about the resurrection of the dead?
options: A gentle, gradual emergence from the graves
A violent overturning and scattering of what is in the graves
A silent rising of souls without bodies
The sealing shut of all graves forever
questions.explanation: Layer 1 and Tabari's analysis explain that 'bu'thira' comes from the root meaning to scatter, overturn, or scatter violently. The graves do not merely open but are scattered and overturned, signaling the comprehensive and irreversible nature of the resurrection.

questions.question: True or false: Wahbah al-Zuhayli explained that the divine name al-Khabir in the closing verse signals that Allah's judgment is not a mechanical weighing of recorded deeds but a comprehensive understanding of circumstances, intentions, and sincere efforts.
questions.explanation: In Al-Tafsir al-Munir, Wahbah al-Zuhayli reflects that al-Khabir signals divine justice tempered with intimate knowledge — Allah judges with full awareness of struggles, intentions, and every hidden act of gratitude or repentance, producing in the believer both accountability and trust.
